questions.q:
What happens to light when it hits a mirror?
a) It is destroyed.
b) It bounces off the surface.
c) It stays inside the mirror.
questions.a: The correct answer is (b). A student who chooses (a) or (c) likely thinks of light as an object that can be "consumed" or "stored" rather than as a wave or ray that travels and redirects upon contact.

questions.q: If you look at a rough wooden desk, is light reflecting off it? Why can't you see your reflection in it like you do in a mirror?
questions.a: Yes, light is reflecting off the desk, but the surface is rough, causing the light to scatter in many different directions (diffuse reflection). A wrong answer suggests the student thinks only shiny surfaces reflect light, failing to realize that all visible objects reflect light to our eyes.

questions.q: If a light ray hits a mirror at an angle of 30 degrees, at what angle will it bounce off?
questions.a: The light will bounce off at 30 degrees. This follows the law of reflection where the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. A student answering incorrectly is likely ignoring the rule that reflection is symmetrical relative to the surface normal.

questions.q: Why do we see a book on a table even if the room is not perfectly lit?
questions.a: We see the book because light sources in the room reflect off the book's surface and enter our eyes. If a student says "the book has its own light," they are confusing self-luminous objects (like stars or bulbs) with illuminated objects.

questions.q: Is it possible to see an object in a room with absolutely no light? Defend your answer.
questions.a: No, it is not possible because reflection requires an initial source of light to bounce off the object; without light, there is no "bouncing" to send information to our eyes. A wrong answer suggests a misunderstanding of the biological necessity of light for vision.

questions.q: Design an experiment to prove that a piece of paper reflects light differently than a polished metal spoon.
questions.a: The student should suggest shining a laser pointer or torch at both surfaces and observing where the light goes. A good answer tracks the focused beam from the spoon versus the scattered glow from the paper. A poor answer fails to include a light source or a way to observe the reflected path.
